concept.name: Binary option
concept.definition: A type of option whose payoff is either a fixed amount or zero, depending on the outcome of a yes/no proposition — typically whether the price of an asset will be above or below a strike at a specified time. It is also called a digital option.
concept.intuition: A binary option is a fixed-odds bet on a market event: pick the right side of the line and you collect the full payout; pick wrong and you get nothing.
concept.mechanics: A cash-or-nothing call pays a fixed cash amount if the underlying finishes above the strike and zero otherwise (asset-or-nothing variants pay the asset). Because the payout is fixed, the option's price — between zero and the payout — reflects the market-implied probability of the event, discounted.
concept.formula: Cash-or-nothing call payoff = Q if S_T > K, else 0, where Q is the fixed payout, S_T the underlying price at expiry, and K the strike.
concept.failure_modes: The all-or-nothing payoff forfeits the entire premium on a narrow miss, and discontinuous payoffs near the strike make hedging unstable (gamma explosion at expiry). The retail binary-options industry has been riddled with unregistered platforms and outright fraud, prompting repeated SEC and CFTC warnings.
concept.misconceptions: That binaries are a simple, low-risk way to trade — typical retail terms embed negative expected value, and the fixed payout caps gains while losses take the whole stake. Also, a binary's price is not 'the probability'; it approximates a discounted, risk-adjusted probability.
concept.example: A binary option pays $100 if EUR/USD closes above 1.0900 on Friday and $0 otherwise; a market price of $42 for the option implies roughly a 42% assessed probability of finishing above the strike.

citations.source: CFTC Glossary: A Guide to the Language of the Futures Industry
